question: For a gynecologic oncology patient undergoing laparotomy who faces up to a 20–30% risk of surgical site infection, which intraoperative bundle elements should I ensure are in place, and how do the standard infection-control practices I follow at the bedside — hand hygiene, personal protective equipment, sterile field maintenance, and sharps/waste handling — fit alongside them to prevent a healthcare-associated infection?
reference: Because laparotomy in gynecologic oncology carries up to a 20–30% surgical site infection risk (infection of the incision or organ space within 30 days), the nurse should verify the additive bundle elements: appropriate antimicrobial prophylaxis (a first-generation cephalosporin for skin flora, with added anaerobic coverage if the bowel is entered during pelvic cancer surgery, and weight-based dose adjustment), skin preparation, avoidance of hypothermia, avoidance of surgical drains, and control of perioperative hyperglycemia. These are layered on top of CDC standard precautions used for every patient — appropriate hand hygiene, personal protective equipment when indicated, category-specific transmission-based precautions, respiratory hygiene, and environmental controls including handling of sharps, laundry, and hazardous waste — plus aseptic and sterile technique with maintenance of the sterile field and correct application/removal of sterile gloves. Together these reduce healthcare-associated infections, which affect over 2 million U.S. patients and cause about 99,000 deaths annually and are largely preventable.
why_both: A gives standard precautions/asepsis; B gives SSI risk, bundle.
source_docs: Guidelines for perioperative care in gynecologic/oncology: Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS) Society recommendations — 2019 update

question: When I prep a patient's abdominal and vaginal surgical site with 2% chlorhexidine gluconate in 70% isopropyl alcohol — or povidone-iodine with alcohol if she's chlorhexidine-allergic — at exactly which points around that skin prep must I clean my hands?
reference: For the antiseptic agent: most current recommendations converge on 2% chlorhexidine gluconate in 70% isopropyl alcohol for surgical site skin preparation, with alcohol-based povidone-iodine substituted for patients allergic to chlorhexidine; alcohol-based combinations (iodophor-or-CHG-plus-alcohol) are considered superior to aqueous povidone-iodine alone, and washing/cleaning the skin around the incision site precedes application. For hand hygiene around that prep, apply the five moments: perform hand hygiene on entry to the room; after touching the patient's surroundings while gathering and setting up the antiseptic supplies; immediately before touching the patient to begin the prep; after the prep if there is body fluid exposure risk; after touching the patient; after touching the patient's surroundings; and again on exiting the room.
why_both: B gives antiseptic agent choice; A gives hand-hygiene moments.

question: For a woman having an abdominal hysterectomy who will have an indwelling catheter placed at the start of the case, does adding a cyanoacrylate antimicrobial sealant over the prepped skin do anything to reduce her risk of the catheter-related urinary infection she may develop postoperatively, and what should I watch for from the sealant itself?
reference: No. Antimicrobial sealants have only been studied when applied to the skin of the surgical site before incision, so they address incisional wound contamination and offer nothing against catheter-associated urinary tract infection. Virtually all healthcare-associated UTIs — the most common healthcare-associated infection, over 30% of infections reported by acute care hospitals — arise from instrumentation of the urinary tract, i.e. via the suprapubic incision or, more commonly, the urethral indwelling drainage tube connected to a closed collection system; CAUTI is associated with increased morbidity, mortality, hospital cost and length of stay, and bacteriuria drives unnecessary antimicrobial use, with drainage systems acting as reservoirs of multidrug-resistant bacteria transmissible to other patients. So urinary infection risk must be managed by catheter-specific measures (avoiding/limiting the indwelling catheter, considering intermittent or external drainage where appropriate, maintaining the closed system, early removal), not by the skin sealant. From the sealant itself, monitor the prepped skin for irritation and allergic reactions, the recognised harms. Also note the sealant evidence base is largely manufacturer-funded, though it applies to adults and children alike, and in the trials both intervention and control skin received the same antiseptic preparation with the sealant simply added.
why_both: A: sealant use site, harms; B: catheter UTI source, burden.

question: During a caesarean hysterectomy complicated by major haemorrhage where we've already run in 2 litres of isotonic crystalloid, 1.5 litres of colloid and emergency group O RhD-negative K-negative red cells, do I need to do anything about the antibiotic given at induction, and when should the surgical antibiotic be repeated?
reference: Yes — an intraoperative redose is indicated. The appropriate antibiotic should have been given within the 60 minutes before the skin incision, and repeat dosing is warranted specifically in the setting of copious/heavy blood loss, prolonged surgery, or after prosthetic (implant) surgery. A woman who has required escalation through up to 2 l crystalloid, up to 1.5 l colloid until blood arrived, and emergency group O RhD-negative K-negative red cells (switching to group-specific units as soon as feasible) clearly meets the 'copious blood loss' criterion, and such a hysterectomy is also likely to be prolonged — so the prophylactic dose should be repeated intraoperatively. Beyond that, prophylaxis should not simply be continued postoperatively as a routine: extended courses are not supported (only arthroplasty is considered for up to 24 hours), and the evidence for prolonged prophylaxis in preventing surgical site infection was judged uncertain enough to require dedicated systematic review.
why_both: A supplies redosing/duration rules; B defines massive-transfusion blood loss.

question: When I'm helping plan care for a woman taken to theatre for uterine tamponade or vessel ligation after drug-resistant heavy bleeding, and who then needs clot prevention cover before discharge, how solid is the trial evidence behind each of those two decisions, and how should that shape what I tell the team and the woman?
reference: Both limbs of her care rest on weak trial evidence, so both are consensus-driven and should be framed that way. For the bleeding: careful clinical examination is needed to establish the cause, and a 2014 Cochrane review of treatment of primary PPH found no trials at all evaluating surgical techniques or radiological interventions in women unresponsive to pharmacological methods — so recommendations on which surgical/radiological escalation to use are based only on observational data and consensus (evidence level 4). For the clot prevention: a Cochrane systematic review of randomised trials comparing a thromboprophylaxis method with placebo/no treatment, and comparing two or more methods against each other, concluded there is insufficient evidence on which to base recommendations for thromboprophylaxis in pregnancy and the early postnatal period; current recommendations were drawn up explicitly recognising this limited evidence, after reviewing existing VTE guidelines. Practically: expect local protocols and senior clinician judgement rather than trial-derived algorithms to drive both the choice of surgical/radiological haemostatic step and the agent, dose and duration of postnatal prophylaxis; document the individualised risk assessment (including the extra VTE risk conferred by her haemorrhage, transfusion and operative delivery), escalate early to senior obstetric/anaesthetic input, and give the woman honest consent information that these are consensus-based rather than trial-proven choices.
why_both: A: no trials for surgical PPH escalation; B: insufficient thromboprophylaxis evidence.
source_docs: GTG52 - Prevention and Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage
GTG37a - Reducing Risk of Thrombosis and Embolism during Pregnancy

question: For a hypertensive woman scheduled for elective hysterectomy who has already no-showed her pre-op assessment visit, how should I handle both her missed appointment and the antihypertensive dose she'll receive on the morning of surgery?
reference: Two linked actions are needed. First, for the missed appointment: because missed appointments correlate with lower adherence to prescribed regimens and are the first signal of dropping out of care entirely, adherence to appointments should be actively monitored. Work with the interdisciplinary team to set up a clinic/office system in which staff telephone the client to remind her of appointments and to follow up on ones she missed; a 2005 Cochrane review concluded that recalling clients who miss appointments may be the single most important intervention for helping clients follow medication prescriptions. Use the call to assess potential barriers to adherence interfering with her treatment plan and to keep her in care, and make any telephone advice consistent with your scope of practice and the College of Nurses standards for telephone advice. Second, when the morning-of-surgery antihypertensive is actually given: use at least two patient identifiers and compare them against the medication administration record; perform the appropriate pre-administration assessment (e.g., review relevant lab values and complete a cardiac/blood pressure assessment) to confirm the right drug, right reason, and right time; double-check and verify the dose calculation, since incorrect calculation causes errors that compromise patient safety; follow a standardized administration procedure and look up current drug information in evidence-based sources; and communicate with her before and after the dose, explaining usage, dose and special considerations and answering her (and family members') questions — which also reinforces the adherence teaching begun on the phone.
why_both: B supplies missed-appointment adherence risk and telephone recall; A supplies safe administration and verification steps.

question: Our team wants to add two extra antiseptic steps to abdominal hysterectomies — a cyanoacrylate film applied over the skin after the alcohol-based chlorhexidine prep and before incision, and an antiseptic/antibiotic applied in the pelvic operative field just before we close — is there solid infection-prevention evidence supporting either step?
reference: Neither step is currently backed by outcome evidence, so neither should be adopted as routine practice in your hysterectomies. The pre-incision cyanoacrylate film (an antimicrobial skin sealant) is a sterile preparation applied as an additional antiseptic after standard surgical-site skin preparation and before incision; it is meant to stay in place, block migration of skin flora from the surrounding skin into the surgical area, and dissolve some days after surgery. It has been shown to reduce bacterial counts on the skin of the operative site, but most studies reported only changes in bacterial colonies and did not examine SSI rates, so its use for SSI prevention remains debated and was not addressed in previously available SSI guidelines — prompting a systematic review by the guideline development group. Similarly, whether applying antiseptics and antibiotics in the operative field before wound closure is clinically and cost effective in reducing surgical site infection rates is still an open research question, not an established recommendation. Practically: keep the standard alcohol-based chlorhexidine or iodine skin preparation (since endogenous skin flora is considered the main source of SSI pathogens), continue proven measures, and treat both add-ons as unproven pending further evidence — ideally used only within audit or trial conditions.
why_both: WHO covers pre-incision sealants; NICE covers pre-closure antiseptics.

question: For a pre-op hysterectomy patient with expressive aphasia who seems not to hear me, how do I actually verify her hearing at the bedside and still get reliable answers from her during my pre-op check?
reference: Do a whispered voice test: with the patient unable to see your lips, whisper a combination of numbers and letters; hearing is considered intact if she repeats at least three of a possible six correctly, then test the other ear with a different combination (also check PERRLA and the cranial nerves affecting hearing and balance if a neurologic cause is suspected). Because expressive aphasia limits her verbal reply, adapt the method: first modify the environment to minimize excess noise and emotional distress (which also makes the whisper test valid), stand in front of her while speaking, present one idea at a time, speak slowly without shouting, and let her respond by writing on a tablet, pointing to a communication board with pictures/letters, flash cards, eye blinking, or hand signals rather than speech. Phrase pre-op questions for simple yes/no answers, but be aware aphasic patients may give automatic responses that are incorrect, so repeat back what she indicates to confirm accuracy, monitor for frustration or anger, solicit family help in interpreting her speech, collaborate with the family and speech therapist on a communication plan, and ensure the call light is within reach with the central call system marked to show she has difficulty with speech.
why_both: A gives whisper-test hearing criteria; B gives aphasia communication adaptations.

question: For a woman with advanced gynecologic cancer who is recovering from palliative pelvic surgery and going home with a peripheral IV for symptom management, how should I prepare and support the family caregiver who will be watching that IV site, so that early vein inflammation is caught and handled appropriately?
reference: Combine caregiver-focused support with concrete site-monitoring teaching. First, assess the caregiver as a client in their own right: evaluate their need for further assistance and their social support network, their physical needs, sleep patterns, and ability to carry out their other responsibilities, and watch for declining health, clinical depression, or increased alcohol/drug use. Respect their values, beliefs, and traditions about illness, family caregiver roles, and decision-making, and build a culturally sensitive plan; arrange practical help (grocery shopping, pharmacy runs, meal preparation), keep them included in decision-making and in honest conversations with the team, listen to their stories, offer presence, active listening and touch, and connect them with community resources and support groups — an exhausted or depressed caregiver cannot reliably monitor a device, so add home nursing visits if their capacity is limited. Then teach the specific signs of phlebitis (inflammation of the vein's tunica intima): localized redness, pain, heat, purulent drainage, and swelling that may track up the vein as a palpable venous cord. Explain prevention that is already built into the plan — smallest outer-diameter catheter, securement technology, avoiding areas of flexion and stabilizing the joint, and following drug-reference parenteral guidelines for dilution and infusion rate to avoid chemical phlebitis from alkaline, acidic, or hypertonic infusates, plus aseptic technique and clean dressings to prevent infectious phlebitis. Instruct them to call rather than self-manage: for transient mechanical phlebitis the nurse may stabilize the catheter, apply heat, elevate the limb, and give analgesics (anti-inflammatory agents if needed), monitoring for 24 hours after insertion and removing the catheter if signs and symptoms persist; for suspected chemical phlebitis the team reevaluates the infusion — different vascular access, a different medication, a slower rate, or a more dilute infusate — and removes the vascular access device if indicated. Reassure the caregiver that reporting a red, painful site is doing everything possible for their loved one, reinforcing their wish to be remembered as a good and compassionate caregiver.
why_both: One gives caregiver assessment/support; other gives phlebitis signs, prevention, treatment.

question: For my post-hysterectomy patient with diabetes and obesity whose incision is healing poorly and who takes antihypertensives, what adherence questions should I ask at her follow-up visit to make sure her blood pressure medications aren't being missed while I address her healing risks?
reference: This patient carries two documented risk factors for delayed wound healing: diabetes, which impairs healing through neuropathy, atherosclerosis (plaque buildup obstructing arterial flow and reducing tissue oxygenation), decreased host immune resistance and increased infection risk; and obesity, which is associated with wound infection, dehiscence, hematoma formation, pressure injuries and venous injuries. Because impaired perfusion and oxygenation underlie the diabetic contribution, keeping her blood pressure controlled matters, so adherence must be actively assessed rather than assumed. Ask: (1) "Have you missed any pills in the past week?" — any self-reported missed dose is consistent with an adherence rate below 60%; (2) "How is your blood pressure doing?" and "Are you having any problems with your medications?" — these probe her perceptions of medication need, effectiveness and safety, and surface medication-specific barriers such as side effects, number of pills daily, dosing frequency, taste, treatment duration and cost; (3) "Are you having any trouble getting and taking your medications?", "Are you able to be regular in your medication taking?" and "What is your routine in taking your medications?" — these assess access and patterns, including logistical barriers (filling prescriptions, getting refills, booking clinic appointments, running out of medication) and inconvenience (carrying medications, frequent clinic visits, public bathroom use). Alongside this, provide the education indicated for her healing risks: diabetes self-management teaching, healthy lifestyle counselling to reduce obesity, and review of medications such as corticosteroids that impair granulation tissue formation, plus alcohol use, which impairs healing and raises infection incidence.
why_both: One gives wound-healing risk factors; other gives adherence questions.

question: For a woman recovering from radical hysterectomy for advanced cervical cancer who has poorly controlled hypertension, how should I frame her ongoing care so that both her suffering from the life-threatening illness and her long-term antihypertensive adherence are addressed?
reference: Combine a palliative care philosophy with community/peer-based adherence support. On the palliative side, care should aim to improve quality of life for both the patient and her family who are facing problems associated with a life-threatening illness, by preventing and relieving suffering through early identification, correct assessment, and treatment of pain and other problems — physical, psychosocial, or spiritual. This means her postoperative pain, nausea, fatigue, fear of recurrence, sexual and body-image concerns, and spiritual distress are all assessed early and treated, and her family is included as recipients of care, not just as visitors. For the hypertension component, adherence to therapy is influenced by health system/health care team factors, condition-related factors, therapy-related factors, patient-related factors, and social/economic factors — all of which are relevant here, since a new cancer diagnosis, added medications, and financial strain each threaten her ability to keep taking antihypertensives. There is substantial evidence that peer support among clients improves adherence to therapy while reducing the amount of professional time needed for chronic condition care, and community interventions produce economic and health benefits by strengthening self-management capacity, promoting the maintenance and motivation required for self-management, and keeping the client active in knowledge of her disease and in acquiring new habits. Practically: refer her to a peer support or community program for both cancer and blood pressure self-management, simplify her regimen and address cost and access barriers, and integrate blood pressure monitoring and education into the palliative plan so symptom relief and chronic disease control are managed as one plan rather than competing priorities.
why_both: One defines palliative care scope; other gives adherence/peer-support strategy.

question: For a woman with diabetes and obesity who is on chronic corticosteroids and now needs an abdominal hysterectomy, can applying a cyanoacrylate-based antimicrobial skin sealant before the incision compensate for her impaired healing risks, and what should I watch for and teach instead?
reference: No. Her diabetes (neuropathy, atherosclerosis with reduced tissue oxygenation, reduced immune resistance, higher infection risk), obesity (infection, dehiscence, hematoma, pressure and venous injury) and corticosteroids (reduced granulation tissue formation) — plus contributors such as older age, alcohol use and stress — are the drivers of poor healing, and no skin product corrects them. The trials of cyanoacrylate antimicrobial sealants studied application to the surgical-site skin before incision as an addition to, never a replacement for, the same standard antiseptic skin preparation given to controls, most of that evidence was funded by the commercial sealant manufacturers, and the recognized harms are skin irritation and allergic reactions (relevant in both adults and children). So continue the unit's usual antiseptic skin prep, inspect her skin for irritation or allergic reaction if a sealant is used, and focus nursing care on education about glycaemic management, healthy lifestyle/weight reduction, exercise, avoiding alcohol, healthy stress coping, and on reviewing whether her corticosteroid or other medications are contributing to delayed wound healing.
why_both: A supplies healing-impairing patient factors; B supplies sealant evidence, harms.
source_docs: WHO Global Guidelines for Prevention of Surgical Site Infection

question: Our patient is having an extended pelvic gynecologic procedure with heavy blood loss and will leave the OR with an indwelling catheter and anticipated clot obstruction — how should I handle her antibiotic dosing and her catheter care to keep infection risk down?
reference: Give the appropriate antibiotic within the 60 minutes before incision, and repeat the dose only because of the copious blood loss and the prolonged operative time (redosing/continuation up to 24 hours is reserved for prosthetic/arthroplasty work, not routine gynecologic surgery) — do not extend antibiotics simply because a catheter is in place. For the catheter, do not clean the periurethral area with antiseptics while it is in situ; routine hygiene such as cleansing the meatal surface during daily bathing or showering is what is appropriate. Bladder irrigation is not recommended routinely, but is acceptable here because obstruction is anticipated from post-surgical bleeding (as with bleeding after bladder or prostatic surgery). Also note there is no recommendation for urinary antiseptics such as methenamine in short-term catheterization.
why_both: A: prophylaxis timing/redosing rules; B: catheter hygiene, irrigation limits.

question: When I need to check a preoperative gynecologic patient's pupils for PERRLA and do the whispered-voice hearing check before her hysterectomy, how close do I actually have to get to her, and how should I handle the fact that I'm moving in that close?
reference: Both of these assessments require you to leave the social zone (four to 10 feet) that nurses normally work within to maintain professional boundaries and move into the client's personal zone (18 inches to four feet) or closer. Pupillary assessment for PERRLA — confirming the pupils are bilaterally equal, round, and reactive to light and accommodation — plus extraocular movement and the other cranial nerves affecting vision, hearing, and balance, requires you to be directly in front of her face, essentially within the space normally reserved for close relationships (less than 18 inches). The whispered-voice test also requires close positioning at the ear, testing one ear at a time and expecting her to repeat at least three of six numbers or letters correctly, then repeating on the other ear with a different combination. Because you are invading her personal zone, explain each step before you begin, tell her you will be close to her face and ear and why, obtain her permission, and watch for signs of psychological discomfort that arise when this zone is invaded. Also consider cultural factors that may affect how acceptable that closeness is, and be aware that in the preoperative area — where she may be gowned, draped, or already sedated — this discomfort can be heightened, so keep her covered and minimize the time spent in that close space.
why_both: A gives eye/ear exam specifics; B gives proxemic zones, discomfort.

question: For a woman undergoing a hysterectomy where a cyanoacrylate-based antimicrobial sealant is painted on the skin before the incision, if she develops a skin reaction to it, can we say she should be routinely sent to a high-dependency or post-anaesthesia care unit rather than the general ward?
reference: No — that cannot be stated as an evidence-based requirement. Skin irritation and allergic reactions are recognised as the possible harms of applying antimicrobial sealants to the surgical site skin before incision, so they should be anticipated, observed for and treated. However, for patients who are not already known to be at high risk of complications or mortality, which patients would actually benefit from postoperative care in a specialist recovery area (high-dependency unit, post-anaesthesia care unit or intensive care unit) is still an open research question rather than a settled recommendation. So a sealant-related skin irritation or allergic reaction alone does not, on current evidence, mandate specialist recovery placement; the decision remains a clinical judgement based on her overall risk and the severity of the reaction (for example systemic allergic features), not a defined criterion.
why_both: A supplies sealant harms; B supplies unresolved specialist-recovery triage evidence.

question: For a same-day-surgery patient who needs both a subcutaneous insulin pen dose and a deltoid IM injection, our cart is out of alcohol prep pads — can we substitute 2% chlorhexidine or povidone-iodine, and how would that change the skin-prep step of each injection?
reference: Yes, with caveats. Alcohol (optimum 60%–95%) is the fastest-acting of the hand/skin antiseptics and has excellent activity against gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria, mycobacteria, fungi, and viruses, but no persistent activity — which is why the standard technique is simply to clean the site with an alcohol swab in a circular motion, place a pad above the site to mark the location, remove the needle cap without contaminating the needle, and proceed. Aqueous chlorhexidine 2%–4% is an acceptable substitute: it has excellent gram-positive and viral activity, good gram-negative activity, and adds persistent activity, but its speed of action is only intermediate — so unlike alcohol it must be applied in the same circular motion and then given adequate contact/dry time before you pinch the inch of subcutaneous tissue and insert at 45–90 degrees (insulin pen) or grasp/spread the deltoid and insert at 90 degrees. Allergic reactions to chlorhexidine are rare but possible, so screen the patient. Avoid iodine (tincture) compounds — they cause skin burns and are usually too irritating; an iodophor (povidone-iodine) is less irritating and also intermediate-acting, so again allow it to dry, and note that patient acceptance varies. Whichever agent is used, the rest of the technique is unchanged: hold the skinfold/muscle fold, inject, count to 10, withdraw, release the fold, activate the safety, and dispose in a sharps container (IM deltoid: follow agency policy on aspiration).
why_both: A supplies antiseptic spectrum/speed; B supplies injection prep steps.
source_docs: Guideline for Hand Hygiene in Health-Care Settings

question: My pre-op hysterectomy patient wears a hijab and declines removing it, and her scheduled morning metoprolol dose is due before transport — how do I handle both the head covering and the beta blocker before she goes to the OR?
reference: Handle these as two separate issues. For the hijab: rather than insisting on removal per the routine preoperative checklist, use cultural negotiation — work collaboratively with the patient and the surgical team to find a mutually acceptable solution, such as leaving the hijab in place and covering it with a surgical cap. Because keeping the head covering does not significantly or adversely affect her treatment plan, the cultural need should be accommodated when feasible, and this is documented and communicated to the OR team. For the metoprolol: complete the pre-administration assessment before giving it — verify the rights of medication administration and check her vital signs, specifically blood pressure and heart rate, against the hold parameters on the MAR (e.g., hold if systolic BP is below 100 or heart rate below a stated threshold). If her values fall outside those parameters, withhold the dose and notify the prescribing provider/anesthesia. If no parameters are written, use clinical judgment and follow up with the provider before administering. Compare her post-dose vitals to the pre-administration baseline to evaluate effectiveness.
why_both: A gives cardiac med vitals/parameters; B gives hijab negotiation.

question: For a hysterectomy on a patient under contact transmission-based precautions, how should the team fit the out-loud confirmation of patient identity and surgical site into the sequence of putting on and taking off the gown and gloves in the operating room?
reference: Combine the two steps in this order: because contact precautions require both gown and gloves to be donned upon room entry (with the gown put on first, as it is usually the first piece of PPE), the team should be fully gowned and gloved before the operative sequence begins; the verbal, out-loud confirmation of the patient's identity and the surgical site is then performed as a team in the operating room immediately before incision — it is not a substitute for, and must be added to, existing local practice, since such oral confirmation was routine at only a minority of hospitals (and formal team briefings at none), so the perioperative nurse must actively prompt it. Speaking the identity/site check aloud while already in PPE means no gown or glove removal is needed to complete it. Afterward, the gown (and gloves) must be removed before leaving the patient's/operating room, with the outer contaminated surface turned inward and rolled into a bundle and discarded into the designated container, to avoid contaminating skin, clothing, or the environment outside the room.
why_both: A: pre-incision oral identity/site check; B: gown/glove donning-removal.
source_docs: Safe Surgery Saves Lives: The Second Global Patient Safety Challenge

question: For an older woman recovering from a hysterectomy who has fragile, easily damaged veins and reduced vision and hearing, how should I adapt her IV site monitoring while she is on the unit, and what support strategy should I build into her discharge plan so she keeps taking her blood pressure medication at home?
reference: On the unit, account for age-related anatomical changes — thinning of the dermal skin layer, thickening of the tunica intima/media, and loss of connective tissue — which make veins fragile and vascular access difficult; also assess her immunity, drug dosage and volume limits, pharmacologic actions/interactions and side effects, and monitoring parameters, plus her cognitive ability, dexterity, and capacity to communicate or learn given her vision and hearing changes, adapting teaching about the IV site accordingly. If any securement or joint stabilization is used near the site, keep it loose enough to permit visual inspection of the access site and vascular pathway, avoid pressure causing circulatory constriction, pressure injury, or nerve damage, remove it periodically to check circulation, range of motion and skin integrity, and never use wooden tongue depressors in immunocompromised patients because of fungal infection risk; keep tubing secured and the dressing dry. For discharge, because her sensory and learning limitations reduce what teaching alone can achieve, link her to peer support and community interventions — peer support among clients improves adherence to therapy while reducing professional time needed for chronic disease care, and community programs improve self-management capacity by sustaining motivation, keeping her engaged in knowledge of her condition, and helping her acquire new habits.
why_both: A gives older-adult IV/vein and learning changes; B gives peer/community adherence support.

question: For a preoperative gynecologic patient whose religious and gender-identity beliefs shape her comfort with genital exposure, how should I adapt the administration of a prescribed vaginal medication and a transdermal patch so that her cultural identity is respected while the technique stays correct?
reference: Recognize first that culture is far more than nationality or ethnicity — it is expressed through religion and spiritual beliefs, gender identity, language, age, socioeconomic status, sexual orientation, geography, education, life experiences, living situation, employment, immigration status, and ability/disability, and that a patient belongs to several overlapping cultures at once (intersectionality), including subcultures based on religion (e.g., Hinduism, Islam, Baptist) and gender (male, female, nonbinary, Two-Spirit). So before touching the patient, ask which of these matter to her: whether she requires a same-gender nurse or chaperone for vaginal administration, whether an interpreter is needed, whether family presence is expected, and whether she wishes to self-administer. Do not assume assimilation — she may have adopted some norms of the dominant culture while retaining others, and pressuring her to conform risks loss of her original identity. Then carry out the technique unchanged: after completing steps 1 through 12 of the oral medication checklist (identification, order and allergy verification, hand hygiene, etc.), for the vaginal route provide full draping and privacy and only the minimum exposure needed; for the transdermal patch, perform hand hygiene and apply clean gloves, remove any old patch, clean the skin with mild soap and water and dry it completely, assess for breaks or rashes and avoid those areas, apply the new patch with gloves while rotating the site per manufacturer recommendations without touching the medication surface, press firmly against the skin about ten seconds, label a piece of tape with date, time and initials placed next to the patch, and perform hand hygiene. Choose a patch site she can keep covered by clothing if modesty is a concern, as long as it is intact skin and consistent with rotation guidance.
why_both: A defines culture/intersectionality; B gives patch and vaginal steps.

question: As we redesign the handoff process for post-hysterectomy patients moving from our perioperative unit to a step-down unit staffed largely by LPN/VNs, which aspects of the care plan must stay with an RN versus what the LPN/VN can contribute, and what dimensions should our team appraise when deciding how firmly to adopt the new handoff practice?
reference: Scope: the LPN/VN may collect and contribute assessment data (e.g., incision appearance, vital signs, pain reports, voiding status) after transfer, but evaluating the plan's effectiveness and modifying outcomes/interventions is outside LPN/VN scope and must be performed by the RN — so the receiving RN retains accountability for reviewing and revising the post-op plan, while the perioperative RN ensures the transferred plan is explicit, evidence-based, accessible to all staff, and tied to identified client goals (the nursing process reduces omissions and duplications, promotes consistent responsive care, improves safety and satisfaction, and supports collaborative management). Appraisal dimensions for adopting the handoff practice: benefits and harms (desirable and undesirable outcomes reported in the literature); values and preferences (importance patients place on the relevant outcomes, from a person-centred perspective); health equity (differential impact across populations/settings and barriers to implementation in a given setting, e.g., a unit with a different staffing mix); the rationale for judging the recommendation strong versus conditional; and practical implementation tips for nurses and the interprofessional team.
why_both: A supplies appraisal domains and strength rationale; B supplies LPN scope limits, nursing-process benefits.
source_docs: Transitions in Care and Services (Best Practice Guideline)

question: For a woman recovering from an abdominal hysterectomy, how should her cardiovascular and peripheral vascular interview findings shape the breathing and mobility teaching I give her to protect her lung expansion?
reference: Combine the two steps. First, the cardiovascular/peripheral vascular interview is not just data collection — the information obtained during that interview process is what the nurse uses to tailor the patient's future education, so her reported symptoms, history, and risk factors determine how you frame and prioritize the postoperative plan. Then apply that tailoring to the interventions that improve breathing pattern and lung capacity after gynecologic surgery: coughing and deep breathing, use of an incentive spirometer, use of an acapella flutter valve to mobilize secretions, increased fluids to thin secretions, frequent ambulation to mobilize secretions, and keeping the head of the bed elevated. Practically, if her interview reveals limited exercise tolerance or leg symptoms, emphasize short, frequent ambulation episodes with assistance plus in-bed incentive spirometry and head-of-bed elevation between walks; if fluid tolerance is a concern from her cardiac history, be deliberate about how you teach the "increased fluids to thin secretions" component and lean more on the flutter valve and deep breathing/coughing. Reinforce the same teaching points at each session, using her interview responses to decide which ones need the most repetition.
why_both: B: interview findings tailor education; A: specific lung-expansion interventions.

question: I'm scrubbing in for an open hysterectomy for ovarian cancer — what alcohol-based antisepsis do I need to complete on myself before gloving, what skin preparation does the patient need, and how should the prophylactic antibiotic be chosen and timed?
reference: Three separate steps: (1) Your own hands — wash with soap and water on arrival in theatre or after donning cap/mask, then perform surgical hand preparation with an alcohol-based handrub before every case: about 5 mL (three doses) into the right palm (use the elbow on the dispenser), dip the right fingertips to decontaminate under the nails for 5 seconds, spread up the right forearm to the elbow with circular movements until fully evaporated (10–15 seconds), repeat on the left hand/forearm, then a further 5 mL rubbed over both hands to the wrists through the palm-to-palm, dorsum, interlaced fingers, finger-backs and thumb-rotation steps (20–30 seconds). Each sequence averages 60 seconds and is repeated as many times as needed to reach the total contact time specified by the product manufacturer; glove only once hands are completely dry. If glove removal leaves powder or biological residue, wash with soap and water. (2) The patient — should shower before surgery with a chlorhexidine-based antimicrobial soap and receive a chlorhexidine–alcohol skin preparation in the operating room (level I evidence of ~40% lower SSI rate versus povidone-iodine; CDC category 1A). (3) Antibiotics — a weight-based first-generation cephalosporin is first choice for hysterectomy, but because this is pelvic cancer surgery anaerobic coverage should be added; give it within 1 hour of incision for peak serum levels, and redose according to case duration and blood loss.
why_both: A: patient skin prep, antibiotic choice/timing; B: surgical handrub technique.
source_docs: Guidelines for perioperative care in gynecologic/oncology: Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS) Society recommendations — 2019 update
WHO Global Guidelines for Prevention of Surgical Site Infection

question: For a post-hysterectomy patient in the PACU who becomes confused and needs a neurologic eye check, what infection-prevention steps should I take around that assessment, and what exactly am I checking in the eyes?
reference: Perform hand hygiene immediately before and after the assessment — it is simple but remains the single best and most effective way to prevent spread of infection, and is a core component of standard precautions along with using PPE (gloves, gown, mask, eyewear) whenever exposure to infectious material such as tears or other secretions is possible, respiratory hygiene/cough etiquette, and proper cleaning of any equipment (e.g., the penlight) used between patients. With clean hands and, if secretion contact is likely, gloves and eye protection, assess the pupils for PERRLA — bilaterally equal, round, and reactive to light and accommodation — and also assess extraocular movement and the cranial nerves affecting vision, hearing, and balance. Compare findings against expected versus unexpected findings, document them, and notify the provider of any unexpected new findings.
why_both: A supplies hand hygiene/PPE precautions; B supplies PERRLA assessment steps.

question: For our inpatient recovering from a laparoscopic urogynecologic prolapse repair who was classified low-risk and managed with early ambulation plus intermittent pneumatic compression, what should we do now that she has a swollen, painful calf suspicious for DVT while awaiting duplex imaging?
reference: Her postoperative plan reflected low-risk prophylaxis — early ambulation with IPC until she could ambulate, with pharmacologic prophylaxis only if her institutional VTE risk score indicated it (individual and surgical risk factors evaluated preoperatively; strong recommendation, high quality). Once DVT (or PE) is clinically suspected, prophylaxis is no longer sufficient: treatment-dose low-molecular-weight heparin should be commenced immediately and continued until the diagnosis is objectively excluded by imaging, unless treatment is strongly contraindicated (e.g., active major bleeding). LMWH is preferred over unfractionated heparin, being at least as effective with lower rates of VTE recurrence or extension (3.6% vs 5.4%; OR 0.68, 95% CI 0.55–0.84), lower mortality (4.5% vs 6.0%; OR 0.76, 95% CI 0.63–0.92) and less major bleeding (1.2% vs 2.0%; OR 0.57, 95% CI 0.39–0.83). Practically: keep mechanical measures and ambulation, notify the surgical team, give empiric therapeutic LMWH, expedite duplex ultrasound, and if the scan is negative stop treatment dosing and revert to risk-based prophylaxis. Note also that if she requires a return to theatre, the enhanced recovery fasting rules apply (6–8 h solids, 2 h clear fluids).
why_both: A gives surgical VTE risk/prophylaxis; B gives suspected-DVT treatment.
source_docs: Joint report on terminology and clinical consensus: Enhanced Recovery After Urogynecologic Surgery (AUGS-IUGA)
GTG37b - Thrombosis and Embolism during Pregnancy Acute Management

question: For an emergency gynae laparotomy on a woman with suspected sepsis from a tubo-ovarian abscess who has a high NEWS2 score, what should I do about the pubic hair over the planned incision and the skin antisepsis, and what does the team need to start while I prepare her?
reference: Two parallel actions. (1) Wound-infection prevention: do not remove the pubic hair at all if it can be avoided; if removal is absolutely necessary for access to the incision, use a clipper — shaving with a razor is strongly discouraged. Prepare the skin with an alcohol-based chlorhexidine gluconate solution (strong recommendation), and do not apply an antimicrobial skin sealant after the surgical skin prep, as this is suggested against for reducing SSI. (2) Sepsis resuscitation: because she is categorised as high risk on NEWS2, she should be given intravenous fluids unless contraindicated (for example cardiac or renal failure); if she had instead scored moderate risk, indicators of organ hypoperfusion such as a raised lactate or acute kidney injury would help decide, though a moderate score alone can be enough to consider fluids. Note that lactate, mottled skin and capillary refill should not drive the decision in isolation — lactate rises for many reasons and mottling is subjective and harder to assess in brown or black skin — and evidence on which fluid type to use is of very low certainty.
why_both: A: hair removal, chlorhexidine-alcohol prep; B: NEWS2-guided fluid resuscitation.
source_docs: WHO Global Guidelines for Prevention of Surgical Site Infection
Suspected Sepsis in People Aged 16 or Over: Recognition, Assessment and Early Management

question: For a post-hysterectomy patient who needs ongoing intermittent catheterization, should I be requesting a prophylactic antibiotic to prevent a catheter-associated UTI, and at exactly which points during that catheterization should I perform hand hygiene — including how the technique changes if she is on Clostridium difficile contact precautions?
reference: No routine antimicrobial prophylaxis. Low-quality evidence shows no benefit of antimicrobial prophylaxis in patients undergoing long-term catheterization, including clean intermittent catheterization: bacteriuria risk fell but symptomatic UTI results were heterogeneous, with no difference in catheter encrustation or adverse events, and one systematic review found increased antimicrobial resistance with prophylactic use (evidence on C. difficile infection was not even available in the short-term catheterization data). Infection prevention therefore rests on technique, not drugs. Hand hygiene for intermittent catheterization should be performed at six points: on entering the room; after touching the patient's surroundings while setting up/preparing for the procedure; before touching the patient; after the procedure/body-fluid exposure risk; after touching the patient's surroundings; and on exiting the room — these map to the five moments (before touching a patient, before a procedure, after a procedure/body fluid exposure risk, after touching a patient, after touching patient surroundings). If she is on C. difficile contact precautions — or if your hands are visibly soiled — use soap and water handwashing rather than alcohol-based hand rub at each of those moments, and combine this with gown and gloves per contact precautions.
why_both: B: no prophylaxis for intermittent catheterization; A: hand-hygiene moments, C. diff technique.
source_docs: Guideline for Prevention of Catheter-Associated Urinary Tract Infections (2009)

question: When preparing a woman for discharge home after a laparoscopic hysterectomy, what should I include about the hospital-issued nonskid slipper socks and staff glove practices in the teaching I give her and her caregiver, and how do I confirm that teaching has actually made them ready to leave?
reference: Combine the infection-transmission points with a formal readiness assessment. On the infection side, the soles of patient-issued nonskid slipper socks carry bacteria and are recognized as an overlooked route of pathogen spread (Welle et al., 2019), so instruct the patient not to wear ward slipper socks onto her bed or take them home into her living space, and to use clean home footwear post-discharge. Also reinforce that gloves are not a substitute for hand hygiene — inappropriate/overused glove wear is documented among care staff (Burdsall et al., 2017; Jain et al., 2017) — and that high-touch personal items such as mobile phones harbour bacterial flora (Morubagal et al., 2017), so her phone and her caregiver's phone should be cleaned and hands washed before touching her incision or drains. On the readiness side, discharge teaching alone is not the endpoint: assess and document readiness for hospital discharge as a distinct construct (Galvin et al., 2017), using a validated tool such as the Registered Nurse Assessment of Readiness for Hospital Discharge scale (Bobay et al., 2018), recognising that nurse-rated and patient-rated readiness often diverge (Mehraeen et al., 2022) and that quality of discharge teaching predicts post-discharge outcomes (Weiss et al., 2017). Assess the caregiver's readiness separately as well (Lutz et al., 2017), and use interdisciplinary/structured follow-up to reduce readmission (Gotlib Conn et al., 2018; Joseph et al., 2016) — including a clear contact pathway if she develops fever, wound drainage, or increasing pain.
why_both: A supplies infection risks (socks, gloves, phones); B supplies discharge-readiness assessment.
source_docs: OpenRN Nursing Fundamentals - Infection Prevention Chapter
Transitions in Care and Services (Best Practice Guideline)

question: For a woman recovering from an abdominal hysterectomy who has hypertension and is taking scheduled opioids with poor intake and limited walking — at what point should I document that she is constipated, and how do the activity and alcohol targets I'm supposed to counsel her on for blood pressure control also support her bowel recovery?
reference: Document constipation when she has fewer than three bowel movements per week; watch for the associated rectal pressure, abdominal cramps, bloating, distension and straining, and recognize her specific risk factors here — opioid use, low food and fluid intake, and impaired mobility (plus chemotherapy if she is receiving it). For her blood pressure, counsel her, in collaboration with the team, to build toward moderate-intensity dynamic exercise 30–60 minutes, 4 to 7 times per week; progressive ambulation as tolerated postoperatively addresses both her hypertension target and the impaired-mobility contributor to constipation. Also assess her alcohol use for quantity and frequency with a validated tool and advise limiting intake to a maximum of one standard drink per day or 9 drinks per week for women (two per day/14 per week for men), which supports blood pressure control and avoids the poor oral intake and dehydration that worsen constipation. Anticipate a bowel regimen and adequate fluid/food intake while opioids continue.
why_both: A gives BP exercise/alcohol counseling; B defines opioid-immobility constipation.

question: In the preoperative bay, a woman scheduled for a hysterectomy has voiced strong concerns about modesty and about being touched or examined by a male caregiver; she also wants her prayer shawl and family present. She now needs a transdermal antiemetic patch placed before transfer to the OR — how should I carry this out?
reference: Honor the modesty concern first: assign a female nurse to place the patch (Muslim clients may express strong concerns about modesty, especially regarding treatment by someone of the opposite sex), expose only the small area needed, keep her draped/curtain drawn, obtain her permission, and let her keep religious articles such as a prayer shawl in place and family nearby, working around them rather than removing them. Then apply the patch by the standard steps: complete the routine medication-administration/identification checks, perform hand hygiene and don clean gloves, remove any old patch, clean the chosen skin site with mild soap and water and dry it completely, assess the skin and avoid any area with breaks or rashes, apply the new patch with gloves on at a rotated site per manufacturer recommendations without touching the medication surface, press firmly against the skin about ten seconds, label a piece of tape with the date, time, and your initials and place it next to the patch, then remove gloves and perform hand hygiene. If only a male nurse is available, explain and ask her preference rather than proceeding without consent.
why_both: B gives modesty/religious needs; A gives patch technique.
